THE J6, K41, AND J33 LANDOWNER GROUP’S INITIAL POST-HEARING BRIEF
	COMES NOW, the J6, K41, and J33 Landowner Group, an alignment of ten separate family groups impacted potentially by Links J6, K41 and J33, its members being:
John L. Kuykendall Family Trust, Jeff Kuykendall, and Lisa Kuykendall Whittlesey;
The Lovell Wilford Kuykendall Estate and the Sandra Jones Kuykendall Estate;
John Clark, Kay Clark, and the Marilyn K. Hawkins Irrevocable Trust;
High Lonesome Ranch Ltd. and LH Haverlah Ranch LP;
Cook Family Partners, Ltd.;
Foster Mitchell Miller and Vicki Miller, FVF Ranches, Ltd., and PTX Ranches, Ltd.;
Matthew and Becke Hillis;
Sherri Ann Fischer and Roy Fischer;
Zentonia, LLC, Thomas Heck, Kerrie Heck and Julie Zente; and
Royce Eugene Gaida and Angelique Marie Gaida, and Gaida Family Ranch LLC,
(together, “The J6, K41, and J33 Landowner Group”), and pursuant to SOAH Order No. 6, file this Initial Brief, and would respectfully show the following:

I.	INTRODUCTION
	The J6, K41, and J33 Landowner Group is made up of families who own properties potentially impacted by this docket, now further bonded by their history, location, and objections to any Routes using said Links J6, K41, and J33. They find themselves in the unenviable position of having the challenge of defending their homes, trying to maintain relationships in a community now divided by this process, all while trying to represent the best of the Hill Country. All of them live in beautiful areas with flowing springs, deep history, cultural resources, and other significant features.  Of the group of families, seven represent multigenerational legacy ranches with everything from traditional cattle operations to high-end beef operations depending on strict biosecurity. Most of the families are neighbors who have literally known each other all their lives. Others are potential lifelong friends who have found the beauty and natural resources of the area compelling and want to make a life here. The common factor is they are stewards of the land and have significant concerns about this process and the fragmentation of the respective properties. The impact of the respective links on their properties is severe. The preference of the group would be to not have to take positions on routing, but the reality presented is that unless there is intervention, this process will go forward; therefore, based on the data and metrics in this matter, there appear to be routes that should be recommended; the same will be addressed herein. 
II.	FACTUAL BACKGROUND
	In this proceeding, Joint Applicants filed 122 proposed routes and 171 alternative route segments. Joint Applicants identified Route 894 as the best-meets route. The J6, K41, and J33 Landowner Group believes that Route 894, under the criteria governing this proceeding, best satisfies the same through its relatively low cost and overall moderation of the effects on community values and environmental integrity; however, the evaluation of Route 894 also shows that it is the least harmful route. The J6, K41, and J33 Landowner Group would also have no objection to Route 487, Route 410, or Route 392. The basis for these positions will be addressed herein.
III.	ROUTING
The Commission must determine which route best satisfies the routing criteria established by statute and rule.
Under PURA § 37.056(c), the Commission must consider several factors when evaluating transmission line routes, including community values, recreational and park areas, historic and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, and the probable improvement of service or lowering of costs to consumers. 
The Commission's routing rule, 16 Texas Administrative Code § 25.101(b)(3)(B), further provides that transmission lines should be routed to moderate impacts on the affected community and landowners to the extent reasonable, while considering engineering constraints and costs. 
In applying these standards, objective routing metrics such as cost, route length, the number of habitable structures affected, compatibility with existing land uses, and engineering feasibility are evaluated. The Commission selects the route that best meets the routing criteria when all factors are considered together.

A.	Statutory Criteria under PURA § 37.056(c)(4) compel the selection of Route 894.
	Under PURA § 37.056(c)(4), the Commission must consider community values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, and the probable improvement of service or lowering of cost to consumers.
		1.	Community Values: Route 894 best protects community values.
	The Commission has interpreted “community values” as a “shared appreciation of an area or other natural or human resource by a national, regional, or local community.” 
	One way to evaluate community values its by addressing the issues raised by the communities themselves. At the three public meetings, Joint Applicants solicited comments and questions from landowners, which they provided in the EA. The community’s concerns included proximity to residences, impact on ranching activities, aesthetics, environmental concerns, and historical resources. Route 894 in large part addresses these issues. 
	First, only two routes in this entire proceeding affect fewer habitable structures than Route 894. Accordingly, Route 894 protects such structures better than any other viable routing option. Second, Route 894 crosses only 162.8 miles of rangeland pasture, despite it being the most prevalent terrain in these proceedings. Routes 572 and CCG, respectively, cross 6 and 10 more miles of this terrain, meaning 6 to 10 more miles of ranching activities would be deeply affected if either of those routes were selected. Third, Route 894 protects the aesthetics of the area by utilizing the J22 Colorado River crossing, which is outside of the one-half mile distance, referred to as viewshed in the environmental assessment criteria of the state parks in the area. Fourth, by avoiding Link J31, Route 894 avoids the only known area of golden-cheek warbler habitat. Sixth, selecting Route 894 would best protect historical resources as it is tied for the least number of cultural sites within 1000 feet of its centerline at only twelve, all while avoiding the historic, recognized Taylor-Rose Ranch on Link G6. Finally, meeting multiple key criteria factors, Route 894 avoids the only known school in the study area, the Florence Independent School District elementary school. 
	When focusing on the community’s primary concerns, Route 894 demonstrates it is the least harmful route as well as the route that best meets the statutory criteria.
2.	Recreational and Park Areas: Route 894 comports favorably with the criteria for analysis routing with respect to recreational and park areas. 
	The avoidance of recreational and park areas is of vital importance to the Commission’s determination of its best-meets route.
	There are two state parks within the study area: the Colorado Bend State Park and the Post Oak Ridge State Park. Critically, Route 894 has no length crossing recreational and park areas. Further, Route 894 does not have any parks or recreational areas within 1,000 feet of the centerline, nor any length identified by Joint Applicants as being within one half mile, which is their metric for determining whether the length would be in the visual foreground of any park or recreational area. 

		3.	Historical and Aesthetic Values
	Under PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(C), the Commission must consider the historical and aesthetic values and the impact of certain transmission line routes on the community. 
a. Route 894 performs favorably on Objective Aesthetics Metrics.
In relation to measuring the aesthetic value under PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(C), the PUC remarked, "[a]esthetic impacts to visual resources exist when the right-of-way, lines and/or structures of a transmission line system create an intrusion into, or substantially alter, the character of the existing view." In determining this impact, the PUC advises, "[t]he significance of the impact is directly related to the quality of the view in natural scenic areas, [and] the importance of the existing setting in the use and enjoyment of an area. 
	Joint Applicants' Data Table confirms that Route 894 performs well on the primary aesthetic metrics. For example, Route 894 has approximately 18.52 miles of right-of-way within the foreground visual zone of Interstate, U. S., and State highways, which is the median for all the filed routes. Further, as calculated by Joint Applicants through evaluation of the length within a half mile of the park or recreational area, a method that is consistent with prior dockets, Route 894 has no length within the defined foreground visual zone of parks and recreational areas with respect to Post Oak Ridge and Colorado Bend State Parks. 
	b. Route 894 minimizes the effects on historical resources.
	Regarding historical resources, Route 894 is among the best-performing routes. Route 894 has only 12 cultural resource sites within 1000 feet of its centerline, tied for the lowest number of any filed route. Similarly, Route 894 actually crosses only two cultural resource sites, which is less than the median of three sites and substantially less than the route crossing the most sites, which crosses twenty. As such, very few routes perform better when considering this criterion. 
		4.	Environmental Integrity
The Commission must factor in preserving environmental integrity when deciding where to put the route. When evaluating the environmental data provided by the Joint Applicants in their data table, Route 894 performs well.
First, despite these routes crossing an area of Texas with hundreds, if not thousands of streams and creeks, Route 894 only crosses 291 streams, placing its performance as above average and well above the median. Second, Route 894 does not cross any upland woodlands or run parallel to streams or rivers for any portion of its length, a rare feat in these transmission line projects. Third, Route 894 uses the Link J22 Colorado River crossing, meaning that it avoids a known golden-cheek warbler mitigation bank, minimizing the negative impact that this line would have on an endangered species. Finally, Route 894 has only one rare or unique plant species within its right-of-way, meaning that the effects of clearing said right-of-way would largely avoid damaging the unique plant life that this State takes pride in growing. In sum, Route 894 strikes a balance between all environmental factors, making it one of, if not the most, environmentally balanced and least harmful routes.

B.	Commission Criteria under 16 TAC 25.101(b)(3)(B) compel the selection of Route 894.
	The Commission's routing rule provides that, considering PURA criteria, engineering constraints, and costs, the line should be routed to reasonably moderate the impact on the affected community and landowners unless grid reliability and security dictate otherwise. The Commission also must consider several paralleling factors and whether the routes conform to the policy of prudent avoidance.
		1.	Engineering Constraints
The Commission must also consider engineering constraints in the selection of its best-meets route.
No party established any engineering constraint rendering Route 894 or any other proposed route infeasible, imprudent, or unconstructible under PURA § 37.056 or 16 TAC § 25.101. The Environmental Assessment reflects that Preliminary Alternative Links were repeatedly refined using updated mapping, stakeholder input, and engineering considerations resulting in the addition, removal, and modification of links before the Application was filed and ultimately producing 171 Primary Alternative Links. Applicants consistently testified that all proposed routes are feasible and constructible and satisfy the Commission's routing criteria. 

		2.	Costs: Route 894 is cost-effective.
	The Public Utility Commission must consider the financial costs of construction when selecting the best-meets routes. When considering construction costs, Route 894’s cost is more than justified by its communal and environmental advantages. 
	The estimated transmission line cost for Route 894 is $1.68 billion, nearly $30 million less than the average route costs of the filed routes in this proceeding. Of the routes less expensive than Route 894, none have fewer habitable structures, none have fewer cultural resource sites within 1,000 feet, none have fewer FM radio towers within 2,000 feet, and only a select few perform better on paralleling, avoiding endangered species, and affecting airports. In sum, given the overall benefits and the relatively low cost, Route 894 is the best meets alternative when considering cost.
3.	Moderation of the Impact on Affected Community: Route 894 best moderates the impact on the affected landowners’ communities.
	Route 894 greatly moderates the impact on the affected communities. This criterion, like community values, is also best addressed by analyzing the public comments provided by the communities throughout the study area. The community’s concerns included proximity to residences, impact on ranching activities, aesthetics, environmental concerns, and historical resources. For the same reasons discussed in the community values section of this Initial Brief, Route 894 minimizes the impacts regarding each of these concerns.	
Several parties argue that Route 894 would have a substantially negative impact on their proposed future development projects; however, historical examples of transmission lines indicate that this is not the case. Applicants themselves identified “countless examples” of residential and commercial developments across their service area growing and thriving despite being immediately adjacent to a transmission line right-of-way. One historical example of a thriving development surrounding an electric transmission line, discussed in these proceedings, is the Domain in Austin, Texas, only a stone’s throw from the venue of the Hearing on the Merits. Potential concerns about future development do not render Route 894 non-viable or subtract from its position as both the clear best-meets route and the least harmful route.
4.	Paralleling: Route 894 performs well with respect to paralleling compatible infrastructure.
The Commission prefers to parallel existing infrastructure when possible. With regard to this criterion, Route 894 fares well.
	Route 894 parallels existing, compatible rights-of-way (including apparent property boundaries) for approximately 43.9% of its length, including 5.66 miles parallel to existing transmission lines, 4.45 miles parallel to public roads and highways, and 91.75 miles parallel to apparent property boundaries, each of which compares well to other filed routes in this proceeding. 

5.	Prudent Avoidance: Route 894 affects a lesser number of habitable structures.
	Under 16 TAC § 25.101, the Commission must adhere to the policy of prudent avoidance, "limiting exposures to electric and magnetic fields that can be avoided with reasonable investments of money and effort." Prudent avoidance requires routing that maximizes distance from habitable structures. Route 894 limits the number of homes exposed to electric and magnetic fields better than nearly every other route filed in these proceedings.
	Applying the Commission’s policy of prudent avoidance to the routes in this proceeding makes clear that Route 894 should be recommended and selected by the ALJs and the Commission. Of the filed routes in the Joint Applicants’ Application, only two routes have fewer habitable structures than Route 894. When considering the lack of added benefits from the routes with more structures, the selection of any route other than Route 894 under the Commission’s policy of prudent avoidance would be largely unjustifiable.
IV. CONCLUSION
 	Route 894 performs better than other alternative routes in nearly every objective criterion provided by the governing statute and rules for this proceeding. It better complies with community values, will have a far lesser effect on environmental integrity and recreational and park areas, and fares better when considering cost, paralleling existing infrastructure, as well as complying with the Commission's policy of prudent avoidance. In sum, the evidence in the record, both qualitative and quantitative, compels the selection of Route 894 as the best meets route and in turn it is the least harmful route in these proceedings. Alternatively, while the J6, K41, and J33 Landowner Group would not object to any route that does not include the links crossing their land, it believes that Route 487, Route 392, and Route 410 are also viable alternatives and would not object to the ALJ's recommendation or the Commission’s selection of the same.
Respectfully submitted,

        a. Route 894 performs favorably on Objective Aesthetics Metrics.

remarked, "[alesthetic impacts to visual resources exist when the right-of-way, lines and/or

structures of a transmission line system create an intrusion into, or substantially alter, the character

of the existing view." 18 In determining this impact, the PUC advises, "[tlhe significance of the

impact is directly related to the quality of the view in natural scenic areas, [andl the importance of

the existing setting in the use and enjoyment of an area. 19

        Joint Applicants' Data Table confirms that Route 894 performs well on the primary

aesthetic metrics. For example, Route 894 has approximately 18.52 miles of right-of-way within

the foreground visual zone of Interstate, U. S., and State highways, which is the median for all the

filed routes.20 Further, as calculated by Joint Applicants through evaluation of the length within a

half mile ofthe park or recreational area, a method that is consistent with prior dockets, Route 894

has no length within the defined foreground visual zone ofparks and recreational areas with respect

to Post Oak Ridge and Colorado Bend State Parks.21

                  4.      Environmental Integrity

         The Commission must factor in preserving environmental integrity when deciding where

to put the route.24 When evaluating the environmental data provided by the Joint Applicants in

their data table, Route 894 performs well.

         First, despite these routes crossing an area of Texas with hundreds, if not thousands of

streams and creeks, Route 894 only crosses 291 streams, placing its performance as above average

and well above the median. 25 Second, Route 894 does not cross any upland woodlands or run

parallel to streams or rivers for any portion of its length, a rare feat in these transmission line

projects.26 Third, Route 894 uses the Link J22 Colorado River crossing, meaning that it avoids a

known golden-cheek warbler mitigation bank, minimizing the negative impact that this line would

within its right-of-way, meaning that the effects of clearing said right-of-way would largely avoid

damaging the unique plant life that this State takes pride in growing. 28 In sum, Route 894 strikes

a balance between all environmental factors, making it one of, if not the most, environmentally

                  Route 894.

         The Commission's routing rule provides that, considering PURA criteria, engineering

constraints, and costs, the line should be routed to reasonably moderate the impact on the affected

community and landowners unless grid reliability                and security dictate otherwise.29 The

Commission also must consider several paralleling factors and whether the routes conform to the

policy of prudent avoidance.

                  1.       Engineering Constraints

         The Commission must also consider engineering constraints in the selection of its best-

meets route.30

         No party established any engineering constraint rendering Route 894 or any other proposed

route infeasible, imprudent, or unconstructible under PURA § 37.056 or 16 TAC § 25.101. The

Environmental Assessment reflects that Preliminary Alternative Links were repeatedly refined

using updated mapping, stakeholder input, and engineering considerations resulting in the

addition, removal, and modification of links before the Application was filed and ultimately

producing 171 Primary Alternative Links. 31 Applicants consistently testified that all proposed

routes are feasible and constructible and satisfy the Commission's routing criteria. 32

         The Public Utility Commission must consider the financial costs of construction when

selecting the best-meets routes.33 When considering construction costs, Route 894's cost is more

than justified by its communal and environmental advantages.

         The estimated transmission line cost for Route 894 is $1.68 billion, nearly $30 million less

than Route 894, none have fewer habitable structures, none have fewer cultural resource sites

the overall benefits and the relatively low cost, Route 894 is the best meets alternative when

considering cost.

                  5.       Prudent Avoidance: Route 894 affects a lesser number of habitable

                          structures.

        Under 16 TAC § 25.101, the Commission must adhere to the policy of prudent avoidance,

"limiting exposures to electric and magnetic fields that can be avoided with reasonable investments

ofmoney and effort. ll41 Prudent avoidance requires routing that maximizes distance from habitable

structures.42 Route 894 limits the number of homes exposed to electric and magnetic fields better

than nearly every other route filed in these proceedings.

         Applying the Commission' s policy of prudent avoidance to the routes in this proceeding

makes clear that Route 894 should be recommended and selected by the ALJs and the Commission.

Of the filed routes in the Joint Applicants' Application, only two routes have fewer habitable

structures than Route 894.43 When considering the lack of added benefits from the routes with

more structures, the selection of any route other than Route 894 under the Commission' s policy of

prudent avoidance would be largely unjustifiable.

IV. CONCLUSION

        Route 894 performs better than other alternative routes in nearly every objective criterion

provided by the governing statute and rules for this proceeding. It better complies with community

values, will have a far lesser effect on environmental integrity and recreational and park areas, and

fares better when considering cost, paralleling existing infrastructure, as well as complying with

the Commission's policy ofprudent avoidance. In sum, the evidence in the record, both qualitative

and quantitative, compels the selection of Route 894 as the best meets route and in turn it is the
